catalog_quote: Table 5. Glottal stop and phonemic stress, with audio examples ... sáyug /ˈsajug/ ‘river’ ... sayúg /saˈjug/ ‘floor’ ... susû /suˈsuʔ/ ‘snail’ ... súsù /ˈsusuʔ/ ‘breast’ ... káun /ˈkaʔun/ ‘eat’ ... kaúnen /kaˈʔunen/ ‘eat’ (OF.INF) ... kaún /kaˈʔun/ ‘go to pick someone up’ ... kaunén /kaʔuˈnen/ ‘go to pick someone up’ (OF.INF) [p. 8] ... It should be noted that both word-initial and word-final glottal stop are retained when prefixed or suffixed, as illustrated by the combination of út-ut ‘suck’ and Actor Focus prefix mag-, and of gawâ ‘do’ and the negative imperative suffix –i (cf. Table 5). Likewise, stress is contrastive, as illustrated in Table 5 by the minimal pairs sáyug ‘river’ vs. sayúg ‘floor’, súsù ‘breast’ vs. susû ‘snail’, and káun ‘eat’ vs. kaún ‘go to pick someone up’. [p. 9]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened all three held (1) 57 pp., LD&C 14, hdl 10125/24912, CC BY-NC open access): p. 9, first paragraph after Table 5, reads exactly as quoted: 'It should be noted that both word-initial and word-final glottal stop are retained when prefixed or suffixed, as illustrated by the combination of út-ut 'suck' and Actor Focus prefix mag-, and of gawâ 'do' and the negative imperative suffix –i (cf. Table 5).[fn 12] Likewise, stress is contrastive, as illustrated in Table 5 by the minimal pairs sáyug 'river' vs. sayúg 'floor', súsù 'breast' vs. susû 'snail', and káun 'eat' vs. kaún 'go to pick someone up'.' The only omission in the reported quote is the footnote marker 12. Table 5 on p. 8 is titled…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive), not fixed: minimal pairs differ only in whether stress is on the penultimate or the final syllable (sáyug /ˈsajug/ 'river' vs sayúg /saˈjug/ 'floor'; súsù /ˈsusuʔ/ vs susû /suˈsuʔ/; káun /ˈkaʔun/ vs kaún /kaˈʔun/). Every IPA form in Lobel et al.'s Tables 3-5 carries stress on either the penult or the ultima, and Salipande 2022 states the window explicitly for the Lopez variety: 'stress falls either on the penultima... or on a closed or open ultima', with length as the main correlate. Suffixation shifts stress rightward in the paradigm examples (káun -> kaúnen OF.INF; kaún -> kaunén).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any of the three sources.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; Lobel et al. note apát 'four' differs from Tagalog ápat only in stress placement (p. 22). Salipande 2022 mentions roots up to five syllables but gives stress only as penult-or-ultima.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (root/citation forms and affixed words, each with audio); Table 5 includes affixed forms showing stress position under suffixation. Lobel 2013:259 calls it 'accent (often called stress, cf. Zorc 1979, 1993)'.
new_statements.identity_note: Lobel et al. 2020 and Lobel 2013 describe Inagta Alabat proper (Alabat Island, Quezon; glottocode alab1246, ISO dul), speakers who migrated from Villa Espina, Lopez. Salipande 2022 describes 'Agta/Inagta Lopenze', the Lopez (Quezon) variety, which he and Lobel treat as the same language (Inagta Alabat-Lopez); no separate glottocode. KWF name for the language is 'Ayta Kadi'.

sources.citation: Salipande, Aldrin Ludovice. 2022. Phonology of Agta Lopenze. Poster presented at the 31st Annual Meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (SEALS 31), University of Hawai'i at Manoa, 18-20 May 2022.
sources.note: Suprasegmental Features panel: 'In Inagta Lopenze, stress falls either on the penultima (i.e., the syllable before the last) or on a closed or open ultima (i.e., the final syllable).... Stress is also phonemic in Inagta Lopenze. Recent studies on Philippine languages revealed that the most reliable determinant of stress is length; the stressed syllable is longer than its unstressed counterpart.' (describes the Lopez, Quezon variety of the same language)
